rows: Upper-limb disorders can affect the neck, shoulders, arms, wrists, hands and fingers.
Repetition, force, posture, duration and insufficient recovery can contribute to risk.
Employers should identify tasks with foreseeable upper-limb risk.
Assessment tools can support structured evaluation of repetitive work.
Workstation, tool and process design can reduce exposure.
Workers should receive information and be encouraged to report symptoms early.
Controls should address the task rather than rely only on individual coping.
Changes in production, equipment or symptoms should trigger reassessment.
A repetitive-task label or symptom report does not quantify upper-limb exposure.
Conclusions require movement, force, posture, frequency, recovery, duration, controls and clinical evidence.
Falls from vehicles are a common workplace-transport accident.
Tasks should be redesigned to avoid climbing onto vehicles where possible.
Safe access should use suitable steps, handholds and working platforms.
Walking and working surfaces should be kept clean and slip resistant.
People should not climb on loads or unsuitable parts of vehicles.
Three points of contact should be maintained when appropriate.
Work at height on vehicles may require collective or personal fall protection.
Vehicle purchase and modification should consider safe access from the outset.
Vehicle steps or a fall-arrest system do not prove that every access task is safe.
Conclusions require task, access route, surface, height, handholds, footwear, load and supervision evidence.
Workplace vehicles should be maintained in an efficient and safe condition.
Manufacturers' maintenance guidance should inform the maintenance programme.
Drivers can carry out basic pre-use safety checks.
More detailed inspections should occur at suitable time or mileage intervals.
Safety-critical defects should be reported and corrected promptly.
Maintenance work should be carried out by competent people.
Records can demonstrate inspections, defects and repairs.
Hired or contractor vehicles still require suitable safety arrangements on site.
A valid road certificate or service record does not prove a workplace vehicle is currently safe.
Conclusions require vehicle type, use, pre-use checks, defects, maintenance, repair competence and verification evidence.
Vehicles falling or rolling during repair can cause fatal crushing injuries.
A vehicle should not be supported only by a hydraulic jack during underbody work.
Suitable stands, lifts or other rated support should be correctly positioned.
Wheels should be chocked or otherwise secured where movement is possible.
Ground and support points should be stable and suitable.
Lifting equipment should be inspected and maintained.
Raised bodies, cabs and components require mechanical support before access.
Workers should be trained in safe lifting and support procedures.
A jack rating or lift inspection does not prove a raised vehicle is safely supported.
Conclusions require vehicle, lifting points, ground, stands, chocks, load, equipment condition and work-method evidence.
